chapters.title: Functions of several variables: partial derivatives, gradient, optimisation
chapters.what: f(x, y) is a landscape. The partial derivatives are its slopes along x and y; together they form the gradient ∇f, which points uphill, steepest, and is perpendicular to the contour lines.
chapters.looks: Contour map (2D) and surface (3D) of the same function; the probe carries the gradient arrow and, in 3D, the tangent plane.
chapters.change: ▶ runs the probe round a circle, or up/down the gradient: steepest ascent crosses every contour at right angles.
chapters.use: Optimisation and machine learning (gradient descent), weather indices, terrain, least-squares fitting.
misc: ∇f = 0 can be a saddle, not only a max or min.
The gradient lives in the xy-plane; it is not tangent to the surface.

examples.title: A saddle: z = x² − y²
examples.world: Hyperbolic-paraboloid shell roofs and the classic crisp shape.

examples.title: Climbing a hill along the gradient
examples.world: Hill-climbing and gradient descent: always step perpendicular to the contours.

examples.title: Rosenbrock's banana valley
examples.world: The standard test of optimisation codes: a curved valley, minimum at (1, 1).

examples.title: Wind chill: a function of temperature and wind
examples.world: The 2001 North American wind-chill index: at −10 °C and 30 km/h it feels like −19.5 °C.
examples.note: x = air temperature T (°C), y = wind speed V at 10 m (km/h).

examples.title: Least squares: the error surface of a line fit
examples.world: Fitting y = m x + c to (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5): the best line is the bottom of this bowl.
examples.note: x = slope m, y = intercept c.

chapters.title: Multiple integration
chapters.what: ∬_D f dA adds f over a region D: volumes, masses, centroids and moments of inertia. Fubini lets it be done as two single integrals, in either order.
chapters.looks: The region as coloured cells (2D) and as prisms of height f standing on it (3D); ▶ refines the cells and the prism sum closes in on the integral.
chapters.change: Switch the integrand to x² + y² or y² and the same region gives its polar or axial second moment.
chapters.use: Volumes and masses, centroids of plates, moments of inertia of beams and shafts, probability over regions.
misc: The limits of the inner integral may depend on the outer variable, never the other way round.
The centroid can lie outside the region (an L-shape).

examples.title: Volume under a paraboloid dome
examples.world: ∬ (4 − x² − y²) over the unit disk = 3.5π.

examples.title: Centroid of a triangular plate
examples.world: The centroid of a right triangle is one third along each leg.

examples.title: A plate whose density grows with x
examples.world: ρ = 1 + x on the unit square: mass 1.5 and the centre of mass shifts to x̄ = 5/9.

examples.title: Polar moment of a round shaft: J = π r⁴/2
examples.world: The torsional stiffness of a solid shaft comes from ∬ (x² + y²) dA.

examples.title: A beam's second moment: I = b h³/12
examples.world: A 2 × 4 rectangle bent about its long axis: I = 2·4³/12 = 10.67.

examples.title: The Gaussian over the plane gives π
examples.world: The bell curve's normalising constant √π comes from this double integral (done in polar coordinates).

chapters.title: Vector calculus
chapters.what: A vector field attaches an arrow to every point. Divergence measures how much it spreads out (sources), curl how much it swirls; Gauss's and Stokes's theorems turn these local rates into fluxes and circulations.
maths: \oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S
chapters.looks: Arrows coloured by strength, streamlines, and particles carried by the flow (▶). In 3D the plane field lifts into a sheet whose height is the divergence.
chapters.change: Move the probe: a vortex has curl everywhere in rigid rotation, but zero curl (except at the centre) for a bathtub drain.
chapters.use: Fluid flow, gravity and electromagnetic fields, heat flux, weather maps.
misc: Circular streamlines do not mean non-zero curl.
Straight streamlines can still have curl (shear flow).

examples.title: Rigid rotation: F = (−y, x) has curl 2
examples.world: A turntable or a rotating tank of fluid: every parcel spins at the same rate.

examples.title: A source: F = (x, y) has divergence 2
examples.world: Water pumped from a well spreads out radially.

examples.title: Earth's gravity: inverse-square and divergence-free
examples.world: Outside the Earth ∇·g = 0; all the 'source' is inside (Gauss's law for gravity).

examples.title: A bathtub drain: circling but irrotational
examples.world: The free vortex v = Γ/(2πr): streamlines are circles yet the curl is zero away from the centre.

examples.title: The magnetic field of a straight wire
examples.world: B = μ₀I/(2πr) in circles round the wire; at r = 1.118 it is 1/r = 0.894 (units μ₀I/2π = 1).

examples.title: Shear flow: straight streamlines, non-zero curl
examples.world: Flow near a wall (u = y): a paddle wheel placed in it turns.
